subject: Biology
title: Gaseous Exchange (KPK Board)
learningOutcomes: Differentiate among respiration, gaseous exchange and breathing.
Describe gaseous exchange in plants through the epidermis, stomata and lenticels during the day and at night.
Trace the path of air through the human air passageway and explain the role of each part up to the alveoli.
Explain the mechanism of breathing (inspiration and expiration) and gaseous exchange in the lungs by diffusion.
Describe the effect of exercise on the rate of breathing and compare the composition of inspired and expired air.
Explain the biological consequences of smoking on the lungs and the circulatory system.
Describe the causes, effects and treatment of bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia, asthma and lung cancer.

sections.heading: Respiration, Gaseous Exchange and Breathing
sections.body: All living organisms need energy for their life-sustaining activities. The ultimate source of energy for life is sunlight: photosynthetic organisms capture it and prepare energy-rich food from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Respiration is an energy-releasing process at the cellular level in which food molecules such as glucose are broken down into simpler compounds like carbon dioxide and water. In aerobic respiration, oxygen is needed for the complete oxidation of food. Gaseous exchange is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment, and it occurs by diffusion. Breathing is the physical process in which animals move air into and out of their body; in higher animals the lungs are the organs of breathing. Respiration and breathing are not the same thing: respiration is a chemical, energy-releasing process inside cells, while breathing is only the movement of air.

sections.heading: Gaseous Exchange in Plants
sections.body: Plants exchange gases directly with the environment through the general surface, the stomata and the lenticels. The outer surface of the root, stem and leaves is the epidermis, and in some parts it carries a thick cuticle; both allow gases to pass. Leaves and young stems have small pores called stomata in the epidermis. Woody stems are covered by bark, which does not allow gaseous exchange, so the bark has special pores called lenticels. During the day all cells respire while the green parts also photosynthesise, so leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. At night there is no photosynthesis but all cells keep respiring, so the cells take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Tilling the soil creates air spaces between soil particles and allows better exchange of gases between the roots and the air.

sections.heading: The Human Air Passageway
sections.body: The human respiratory system has two main components: the air passageway and the lungs. The air passageway is the set of connected tubes through which air reaches the lungs and leaves them again. Air follows this path: external nostrils, nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and finally the alveoli. In the nasal cavities the air is warmed, moistened and freed from dust by the hairs and the mucous membrane. The pharynx is a muscular passage about 4.5 inches long; its tonsils and adenoids trap and filter microorganisms. The larynx (voice box) leads into the trachea through the glottis, which is guarded by the lid-like epiglottis that keeps food out. The trachea (wind pipe) has a ciliated, mucus-secreting inner surface and 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings that keep it open. It divides into two bronchi, which divide into smaller bronchi and then into bronchioles of 1 mm or less with no cartilage. Each bronchiole ends in a cluster of alveoli, the thin-walled pouches covered with blood capillaries where gaseous exchange takes place.

sections.heading: The Lungs and the Pleura
sections.body: The lungs lie in the chest cavity (thorax). They are enclosed from above and the sides by the chest wall, and the diaphragm lies below them. Each lung is enclosed in a double membrane called the pleura, which contains pleural fluid that makes the expansion and contraction of the lungs easy. The size of the lungs of an organism is related to its activities and body form, which is why the cheetah and the elephant have large lungs.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Breathing
sections.body: Breathing has two phases that follow each other continuously: inspiration (taking in air) and expiration (letting out air). Air moves in when the pressure in the lungs is lower than the pressure outside the body, and moves out when the pressure in the lungs is greater than the atmospheric pressure. During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and becomes flat, and the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract so that the ribcage expands. The volume of the chest cavity increases, the pressure on the lungs decreases and air rushes in. During expiration the diaphragm and rib muscles relax, the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped again and the ribcage goes down. The volume of the chest cavity decreases, the pressure on the lungs increases and the air is expelled.

sections.heading: Gaseous Exchange in the Lungs
sections.body: The alveoli are very thin-walled and are covered with a network of blood capillaries, so they are an excellent site for gaseous exchange. The blood entering the capillaries has a low oxygen concentration, while the inhaled air in the alveoli has a higher oxygen concentration, so oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the capillaries. The carbon dioxide concentration in the blood of the capillaries is higher than in the alveoli, so carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is breathed out. Deoxygenated blood reaches the alveolus through an arteriole and oxygenated blood returns through a venule.

sections.heading: Breathing Rate and Composition of Air
sections.body: At rest the rate of breathing is 15 to 20 times per minute. During exercise more oxygen is needed to oxidise glucose for energy, so more carbon dioxide is produced and collects in the blood. The medulla of the brain, the breathing centre, detects the extra carbon dioxide and sends nerve impulses at greater speed to the diaphragm and rib muscles, so the rate and depth of breathing rise to 30 to 40 times per minute. Inspired air contains 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide, with variable water vapour and temperature. Expired air contains 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide, is saturated with water vapour and is at 38 °C.

sections.heading: Biological Consequences of Smoking
sections.body: Tobacco smoke contains over 4,000 chemicals, of which more than 69 are known carcinogens (cancer-causing chemicals). The most crucial risk of smoking is cancer. Tar makes up most of the particulate matter inhaled by a smoker; it contains many carcinogens, stains the teeth, fingers and lung tissue, and increases mucus and phlegm. Nicotine increases heart rate and blood pressure, narrows the blood vessels, damages muscles, disturbs hormones and metabolism, and increases platelet stickiness, which can cause blockage and coronary diseases. Carbon monoxide is formed when a cigarette is lit; it combines with red blood cells and prevents oxygen transportation, and together with other toxins it inflames the airways and impairs lung function. Benzene causes blood cancer (leukaemia), formaldehyde causes cancers and respiratory, skin and gastrointestinal problems, thirty different metals are found in the smoke, and all the radioactive compounds are carcinogens. Breathing smoke-laden air by non-smokers is passive smoking. It irritates the eyes and throat and can cause cancer, so smoking is banned in public places and on public transport, and the WHO has called on governments to stop tobacco advertisements.

sections.heading: Respiratory Disorders
sections.body: Bronchitis is inflammation or infection of the lining of the bronchi or bronchioles caused by viruses, bacteria and their particles; it reduces air flow and forms mucus. Short-term bronchitis resolves in two weeks; if it does not, antibiotics (bacterial) or anti-viral medicines (viral) are given. Emphysema is a severe lung disease in which the walls of the alveoli are damaged; cigarette smoke is the most common cause, the effects are permanent and irreversible, and the patient has shortness of breath. Pneumonia is inflammation of the lungs due to infection in the alveoli, which fill with pus; it is caused by bacteria, viruses or fungi, starts as a cold followed by high fever (up to 104 °F), shaking chills and a cough with sputum, and spreads by droplets of coughs and sneezes. Asthma is swelling of the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles, which narrows the passage; allergens such as pollens, cold and smoke trigger recurring attacks of shortness of breath, wheezing, coughing and chest tightness, treated with bronchodilators in inhalers. Lung cancer is more common in men; its causes are smoking, industrial carcinogens and air pollution, its symptoms are cough with sputum, breathlessness and pleural chest pain, it shows no symptoms early, becomes painful, incurable and fatal when advanced, and is treated with surgery, chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

sections.heading: Science, Technology and Society
sections.body: Mechanical ventilation is a form of artificial respiration in which a breathing machine pushes air into the lungs of a patient whose lungs are not functioning properly. It has controls for the rate and size of each breath, humidifies, warms and moistens the air, traps unused moisture in its special tubing, and ensures that adequate oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide is exhaled. Fossil fuel exhausts contain carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde and soot; breathing them increases the risk of lung cancer and of non-cancerous conditions, especially asthma. A home ventilation system supplies fresh air, removes stale and polluted air and keeps humidity at proper levels, which helps reduce allergy and asthma symptoms.

definitions.definition: An energy-releasing process at the cellular level in which food molecules such as glucose are broken down into carbon dioxide and water.
The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment, which occurs by diffusion.
The physical process in which animals move air into and out of their body to get oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
The movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Small pores in the epidermis of leaves and young stems through which air moves in and out.
Special pores in the bark of woody stems that allow gaseous exchange with the environment.
The connected tubes through which air reaches the lungs and leaves them after gaseous exchange.
A lid-like structure that guards the glottis and prevents food from entering the larynx.
Microscopic, thin-walled pouches at the ends of the bronchioles, covered with blood capillaries, where gaseous exchange occurs.
The double membrane that encloses each lung and contains pleural fluid.
The taking in of air into the lungs.
The letting out of air from the lungs.
Cancer-causing chemicals, such as those present in tobacco smoke.
The breathing of smoke-laden air by non-smokers.
Inflammation or infection of the lining of the bronchi or bronchioles.
A severe lung disease in which the walls of the alveoli are damaged.
Inflammation of the lungs due to infection in the alveoli, which fill with pus.
Swelling of the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles that reduces the inner passage and causes shortness of breath.
Allergy-causing factors such as pollens, cold, smoke or other chemicals in the air.
Medicines containing chemicals that dilate the bronchioles, given to asthma patients as inhalers.
A form of artificial respiration that uses a breathing machine to assist patients with breathing.

examTips: Respiration (chemical, energy-releasing, inside cells) and breathing (physical movement of air) are not the same — differentiating among respiration, gaseous exchange and breathing is a favourite question.
Learn the path of air as one chain: Nostrils → Nasal cavities → Pharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli.
In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and becomes flat and the ribcage expands; in expiration both relax. Remember volume and pressure change in opposite directions.
Memorise Table 10.1: oxygen 21% → 16%, carbon dioxide 0.04% → 4%, expired air saturated with water vapour and at 38 °C.

Prepare the disorders table line by line: bronchitis (lining of bronchi), emphysema (alveoli walls damaged), pneumonia (alveoli filled with pus), asthma (swollen bronchial walls), lung cancer (smoking is the main contributor).

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore each labelled part of the human air passageway and lungs (Fig. 10.4). Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: External Nostrils
hotspots.fact: Two openings on the ventral side of the head that let air from outside into the nasal cavities.

hotspots.label: Nasal Cavity
hotspots.fact: The air is warmed, moistened and freed from dust by the hairs and the mucous membrane.

hotspots.label: Pharynx
hotspots.fact: A muscular passage about 4.5 inches long whose tonsils and adenoids trap and filter microorganisms.

hotspots.label: Epiglottis
hotspots.fact: A lid-like structure that guards the glottis and prevents food from entering the larynx.

hotspots.label: Larynx
hotspots.fact: The voice box, which surrounds the upper part of the trachea.

hotspots.label: Trachea
hotspots.fact: The wind pipe, kept open by 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings and lined with ciliated, mucus-secreting cells.

hotspots.label: Bronchus
hotspots.fact: Each of the two branches of the trachea enters the lung on its own side.

hotspots.label: Lung
hotspots.fact: The lungs lie in the chest cavity, enclosed by the pleura, with the diaphragm below them.

hotspots.label: Diaphragm
hotspots.fact: A dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle that separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which process is an energy-releasing process at the cellular level?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Respiration is the energy-releasing process in which food molecules such as glucose are oxidised inside cells.

practiceQuestions.prompt: By which process does gaseous exchange occur?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gaseous exchange occurs by diffusion, from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which special pores in woody stems allow gaseous exchange through the bark?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bark does not allow gaseous exchange, so woody stems have special pores called lenticels in the bark.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the structures through which air flows in the human body?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Air passes from the nasal cavities into the pharynx, larynx and trachea, which divides into bronchi and then bronchioles.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Food is prevented from entering the larynx by the:
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lid-like epiglottis guards the glottis and prevents food from entering the larynx.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The diaphragm is flat and the ribs move out. This occurs during:
practiceQuestions.explanation: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and becomes flat and the ribcage expands.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A smoker's blood carries less oxygen because one chemical of cigarette smoke combines with red blood cells. Which one?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carbon monoxide combines with red blood cells and prevents oxygen transportation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In which disease are the walls of the alveoli damaged?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Emphysema is a severe lung disease in which the walls of the alveoli are damaged; cigarette smoke is its most common cause.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Breathing and respiration mean exactly the same thing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Respiration is a chemical, energy-releasing process inside cells, while breathing is only the physical movement of air.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At night, plant cells take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
practiceQuestions.explanation: At night there is no photosynthesis, but all cells carry out respiration, so they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Expired air contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inspired air.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Inspired air has 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide; expired air has 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Asthma is treated with bronchodilators given as inhalers.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bronchodilators contain chemicals that dilate the bronchioles and are given to asthma patients in the form of inhalers.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The muscular, dome-shaped sheet below the lungs is called the ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle that separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Gaseous exchange in the lungs takes place in the ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The thin-walled alveoli, covered with blood capillaries, are the site of gaseous exchange.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At rest, the rate of breathing is ____ times per minute.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Under resting conditions the rate of breathing is 15 to 20 times per minute.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the structures in the order through which air passes from outside the body to the alveoli.
sequencingActivity.explanation: Air enters through the external nostrils, passes the nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx and trachea, which divides into bronchi and bronchioles that end in the alveoli.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A student's diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles contract. Which sequence of changes follows?

options: Chest volume decreases, lung pressure rises, air is expelled
Chest volume increases, lung pressure falls, air rushes in
Chest volume increases, lung pressure rises, air is expelled
Chest volume stays the same, lung pressure falls, air rushes in

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and rib muscles increases the volume of the chest cavity, so the pressure on the lungs drops below the atmospheric pressure and air rushes in.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A long-time smoker has shortness of breath because the walls of his alveoli are damaged, and the damage cannot be undone. Which statement is correct?

options: He has asthma, which is cured completely by inhalers
He has emphysema; the effects are permanent but stopping smoking can reduce further damage
He has bronchitis, which resolves without treatment in two weeks
He has pneumonia, which is treated with bronchodilators

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Damaged alveolar walls with permanent effects point to emphysema, whose most common cause is cigarette smoke; stopping smoking can reduce further damage.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which statement best explains why a smoker is at greater risk of coronary disease?

options: Tar stains the teeth and fingers
Nicotine increases platelet stickiness, which can cause blockage in the blood vessels
Benzene dissolves in the lung tissue
Formaldehyde removes oxygen from the air

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure, narrows the blood vessels and increases platelet stickiness, which can cause blockage and coronary diseases.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: During exercise, the medulla detects extra ______ in the blood and sends impulses faster to the diaphragm and rib muscles.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: More glucose is oxidised during exercise, so more carbon dioxide collects in the blood; the medulla detects it and raises the rate and depth of breathing.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Expired air has less oxygen than inspired air because the oxygen is destroyed in the lungs.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: False — oxygen is not destroyed; it diffuses from the alveoli into the blood of the capillaries, so the air breathed out has less oxygen.
